parts.label: (a)
hints: Hint 1: Look at the form $V = V_0 \sin(\omega t)$ and pick out what the number 320 tells you about the maximum size of the swing.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Spot the peak value**
For a sine supply $V = V_0 \sin(\omega t)$, the number in front is the peak p.d. $V_0$. Here $V_0 = 320\text{ V}$. The r.m.s. value is the equivalent d.c. value that gives the same heating power.

Step 2: **Convert peak to r.m.s.**
For a sinusoid: $$V_{rms} = \frac{V_0}{\sqrt{2}}$$ So: $$V_{rms} = \frac{320}{\sqrt{2}} \approx 226\text{ V} \approx 230\text{ V}$$

parts.label: (b)
hints: Hint 1: Compare $V = 320\sin(100\pi t)$ with the standard $V = V_0\sin(\omega t)$ to identify the angular frequency $\omega$.
Hint 2: Remember $\omega$ is linked to frequency $f$ and period $T$ by $\omega = 2\pi f = 2\pi/T$ - rearrange to find $T$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Identify angular frequency**
Comparing with $V = V_0 \sin(\omega t)$ gives: $$\omega = 100\pi\text{ rad s}^{-1}$$ This tells you how fast the sine oscillates.

Step 2: **Link omega to period**
You know: $$\omega = 2\pi f = \frac{2\pi}{T}$$ Rearrange for $T$: $$T = \frac{2\pi}{\omega} = \frac{2\pi}{100\pi} = \frac{2}{100}$$ $$T = 0.020\text{ s}$$ That is 20 ms, so frequency is 50 Hz, the UK mains frequency.

parts.label: (c)(i)
hints: Hint 1: Think about what a single diode in series does - does it let both halves of the a.c. through or does it block one half?
walkthrough:
Step 1: **What a single diode does**
A diode conducts in the forward direction only and blocks reverse current. In series with R it therefore passes current for only one half of each a.c. cycle and gives zero p.d. across R for the other half. With one diode this is called half-wave rectification.

parts.label: (c)(ii)
hints: Hint 1: Start from the period you found in (b) - how many full 20 ms cycles fit into 0 to 40 ms, and where does the sine start positive?
Hint 2: Think when the diode is forward biased and when it blocks, so for which 10 ms intervals is $V_R$ a sine hump and for which is it zero.
Hint 3: Recall the peak height for $V_R$ when conducting - what was $V_0$ from the original equation and at what times do the peaks occur?
parts.proper_answer: Two positive sine humps only, peak $320\text{ V}$, zero otherwise: hump 0 to 10 ms peaking at 5 ms, zero 10 to 20 ms, hump 20 to 30 ms peaking at 25 ms, zero 30 to 40 ms.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Set the time scale**
From (b) $T = 20\text{ ms}$. So 0 to 40 ms is exactly two cycles. The supply $V = 320\sin(100\pi t)$ starts at 0, goes positive for the first half-cycle (0 to 10 ms), negative for the second half (10 to 20 ms), then repeats.

Step 2: **Keep only one half**
Assume the diode conducts on the positive half. Then across R: $$V_R = V \text{ for } 0<t<10\text{ ms, } 20<t<30\text{ ms}$$ $$V_R = 0 \text{ for } 10<t<20\text{ ms, } 30<t<40\text{ ms}$$ There is no negative part - the graph stays at or above zero.

Step 3: **Draw the correct shape and size**
Sketch half-sine pulses with peak $320\text{ V}$ at $t = 5\text{ ms}$ and $t = 25\text{ ms}$, falling back to zero at 10 ms and 30 ms, with flat $V_R = 0$ lines joining the pulses. The shape is the top half of a sine wave, not triangular.

parts.label: (c)(iii)
hints: Hint 1: Think which component can store charge when $V_R$ is high and release it when the diode blocks, to fill in the zero gaps.
parts.proper_answer: Connect a capacitor in parallel with resistor R.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Smooth with stored charge**
A capacitor in parallel with R charges up to the peak when the diode conducts, then discharges slowly through R when the diode blocks. This holds $V_R$ up and smooths the gaps between pulses toward steady d.c.
